newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU seeks to reassure rejected easterners.
newsitem.headline: EU seeks to reassure rejected easterners.

text.p: The European Commission will try next week to reassure five dejected Eastern European countries they are not being left out in the cold by the EU's grand plan to expand beyond the former Iron Curtain.

The Commission, which will on Wednesday publish long-awaited advice to EU governments on how suitable 10 eastern countries are for the rigours of EU membership, will say that Poland, Hungary, the Czech Republic, Slovenia and Estonia fit the bill.

In a bid to reassure a bitterly disappointed Latvia, Lithuania, Slovakia, Romania and Bulgaria that they are still on track to join, the Commission has conceived a cosy waiting room where they can prepare for the economic and political demands of membership.
"It will keep the applications warm. It's a kind of hot waiting room rather than a refrigerator," one EU official said on Friday.
Under the plan each reject's application will remain on the table and will be reviewed every year. They will each receive a timetable for meeting the criteria for joining.

Whether Turkey, whose application is still being shunned on account of its human rights record, will be involved in some way in a standing European conference grouping all the countries on the membership track is still a matter of discussion, EU officials said.
The five eastern rejects' disappointment is sharpened by the fact that it is their second rejection by the west in a matter of days.
At a historic summit in Spain this week, NATO invited only three countries -- Poland, the Czech Republic and Hungary -- to start negotiations leading to planned admission in 1999.
The European Commission decision, reached in principle on Thursday, is expected to be finalised in Strasbourg next Tuesday, a day before the EU executive unveils its advice to EU governments.
Even then the EU's expansion project will not be home and dry, as EU governments, which have the final say over who should be admitted to talks, are divided.

French President Jacques Chirac, a champion of the EU's enlargement to the former communist bloc, insists talks with all 10 applicants should start in parallel while Luxembourg, the current EU president, has made no secret of its wish for a smaller expansion than the Commission plans.
The Nordic countries are keen to see all three Baltic States negotiating EU entry at a time when they are trying to distance themselves from their Soviet past.
Smaller countries already in the EU favour a smaller enlargement, for fear of losing power in the institutional overhaul a larger enlargement would entail.
EU leaders failed to agree at their June 16-17 Amsterdam summit on the reforms needed to loosen the bloc's decision-making procedures in preparation for enlargement.
Under the fudge agreed at Amsterdam the EU must hold a new treaty-revising conference if it expands to more than 20 members.
The Commission also says that Cyprus, which has already been judged fit for EU membership talks, should negotiate along with the five east Europeans, taking the EU's membership to 21.
